title: Compassion in practice
hook: daya is the mother of dharma in the Japji

segments.voice: Yesterday, contentment: santokh quiets the hunger for more, but not the hands. Your line was content and working. Did you finish one task and call it enough? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-seven.

An old Indian picture of the world: the earth rests on the back of a great bull. It holds everything up. Solid, simple, done. Then someone asks the obvious question a child would ask. And what is the bull standing on? In the Japji, Guru Nanak asks it. In paraphrase: how much weight is on that bull, and what holds it up from below? He doesn't throw the old picture away. He opens it up, and puts something surprising inside. Today: compassion in practice, and what the bull really is.
screen: `THE EARTH ON A BULL'S BACK.` → `WHAT IS THE BULL STANDING ON?` → `COMPASSION IN PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: First, the line. In the sixteenth pauri of the Japji, Guru Nanak gives the answer, in paraphrase: the bull is dharma, the son of compassion; it is contentment that patiently holds the earth in its place. In the original, dhaul dharam daiaa kaa poot. The bull is righteous living, dharma. And dharma has a mother: daya, compassion. Yesterday's santokh shows up again, too, as the thread that keeps it all steady. Second, what that order means. Compassion comes first. Rules, duties, right conduct: all of it is born from caring. If dharma loses its mother, it becomes a set of rules that can be kept coldly, even cruelly. If it keeps her, the rules stay warm. Third, the same pairing turns up again. In Asa di Var, offered a ritual sacred thread, Guru Nanak describes the only thread he'd wear. In paraphrase: make compassion the cotton, contentment the thread, self-restraint the knots, and truth the twist; that is the thread for the soul, and if you have it, put it on me. Compassion again sits at the bottom, as the raw cotton everything else is spun from. Fourth, in practice. Compassion here isn't a mood. It's what moves a hand. In Sikh life it can look like a langar ladle, a meal carried to a neighbor, a hard truth said gently instead of cruelly. It isn't softness, either; a Sikh may stand firm against wrong, and still let compassion set the tone. So when the order gets confusing, when a rule and a person seem to pull in different directions, the Japji gives a place to start. Ask the mother before you ask the son. Compassion first.
screen: `THE BULL IS DHARMA, SON OF COMPASSION.` · `RULES BORN FROM CARING STAY WARM.` · `THE THREAD: COMPASSION THE COTTON.` · `COMPASSION MOVES A HAND.` · then, large: `DHAUL DHARAM DAIAA KAA POOT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: act with compassion. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person you'll see or talk to today. Someone tired, maybe, or difficult, or easy to overlook. Breathe in, and ask: what is it like to be them today? Breathe out, and let a little of the answer reach you. Then choose one small act that would help them, something your hands or your voice could actually do before tonight. Keep it simple enough that you'll really do it. The bell holds the time.
Compassion in practice. Daya: in the Japji, the mother of dharma; right conduct is born from caring, and caring shows up as something done. Today's word.

Your line: compassion first. Today, before you decide whether someone is right or wrong, ask what they might be carrying. Then do the small kind thing you chose. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of daya, compassion, as a core virtue and express it in seva: serving langar, caring for the sick and helping those in need, whoever they are.

original.note: Gurmukhi: daya, compassion; in the Japji, the mother of dharma.

what a scholar hears: Japji pauri sixteen, dhaul dharam daiaa kaa poot, turns an old cosmic bull into ethics, and Asa di Var's daiaa kapaah santokh soot makes compassion the cotton of the soul's thread.

Editor: removed the Kabir couplet. The version quoted (where there is compassion, there is dharma ... where there is anger, there is death) is the popular doha; the Granth's own salok at Ang 1372 reads, as far as the editor can tell, giaan/dharam, jhooth/paap, lobh/kaal, khimaa/aap (wisdom, falsehood, greed, forgiveness), so it did not support the lesson. Replaced it with Guru Nanak's sacred-thread salok (Ang 471, daiaa kapaah santokh soot), and updated the match pair, myth item, screen head, trapdoor and sources. Please confirm Ang 471 and the paraphrase.
Editor: the hook now calls the bull 'an old Indian picture' rather than dating it to Guru Nanak's time; the Japji's question about the bull is in the text.
Gurmukhi ਦਇਆ and pronunciation should be checked.
